headline: Tentai is from Middle Chinese 天體, analysable as 天 (ten, “heaven”) plus 体 (tai, “body”).
Ren'ai is from Middle Chinese 戀愛.
ブザー is from the spelling pronunciation of English buzzer.
カメラマン is borrowed from English cameraman.
レース covers “race” and “lace”, and the source borrows both from English.
ストライキ is borrowed from English strike, a doublet of ストライク.
Genso is 元 (gen, “element”) plus 素 (so, “element”), and a calque of Dutch hoofdstof.
Munashii is むな (muna, “cavity, void, open space”) plus the adjective-forming suffix しい (shii).
パジャマ is from American English pajamas, treating the s as a plural.
Genshu is from the Middle Chinese compound 元首, literally “first, prime + head”.
Usotsuki is 嘘 (uso, “a lie”) plus つく (tsuku, “to tell (a lie)”), literally “lie teller”.
Ikuta is a literal reading of 幾多 (ikusobaku).
Kyōwa is from Middle Chinese 共和, and Mitsukuri Shōgo later used it for the United States.
Dō, “trunk”, is from Middle Chinese 胴 (MC duwngH).
Nengō is from the Middle Chinese compound 年號, literally “year + call”.
Odoodo shifted from earlier おづおづ (ozuozu), a reduplication of Old Japanese 怖づ (“to be intimidated, to hesitate”).
Jari may be a shift from the sazare of 細石 (sazareishi, “gravel, pebble”), but jari is cited to 1619 and zari only to 1677.
Uwaki is 上 (uwa, “over”) plus 気 (ki, “spirit”), with 浮 an example of jukujikun.
Kokoroe is the continuative stem of the verb 心得る (kokoroeru, “to know, understand”).
インターナショナル is from English international.
Ninshiki is a compound 認識, literally “know, recognize; know, remember”, which the source compares to Mandarin rènshi.
Tobira is 戸 (to, “door”) plus 片 (hira, “broad, flat thing”), with hira voiced to bira by rendaku.
Fudōsan was coined by Mitsukuri Rinsho as a translation of French immobilier.
Horobiru is a shift from the Classical Japanese verb 滅ぶ (horobu).
カテゴリー is from German Kategorie.
ダース is borrowed from English doz, short for dozen, and is a doublet of ダズン (dazun).
In bōgai, 害 is a daiyōji replacing 碍.
メディア is an internationalism, pointing to English media.
Fukeiki is 不 (fu-) plus 景気 (keiki).
Heishi is 兵 (hei, “soldier”) plus 士 (shi, “warrior”).
Shin'nyūsei is 新入 (shinnyū, “newly-entered”) plus 生 (-sei, “student”), first cited to 1899.
